title: Huawei's Ascend chose the hardest road: no compatibility with Nvidia
dek: For three or four decades Chinese IT followed; Ascend is Huawei's first product that doesn't solve a chokehold problem but walks into uncharted territory, starting level with Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets harder the longer you do it.
why: The first half is about how the book was written, with low information density; from the two pivotal decisions at Ascend's founding, Fang Xingdong supplies plenty of frontline detail and judgment that only exist in the book.
who: Founders, investors and engineers watching domestic compute, the semiconductor supply chain and AI infrastructure — especially anyone trying to understand how Ascend's path differs from Nvidia's.
skip: The first ~13 minutes cover the origins and interview process of the six books, with little bearing on investment judgment.

points.h: Ascend's harshest decision was not to be compatible with Nvidia
points.body: At Ascend's founding there were two choices. The first was whether AI chips should be specialized or general-purpose; Liao Heng, as chief scientist, judged that AI should be a general-purpose product, and the architectural choice has been proven right today. The second was harder: whether to be compatible with Nvidia. Many domestic chips chose compatibility, with the benefit that Nvidia's existing ecosystem and tools could all be shared. But Xu Zhijun was firm from the start: they had to take a different path. Fang Xingdong sees this choice as enormously bold at the time, and it faced huge challenges many times along the way — because the entire Chinese IT industry has been a follower industry for three or four decades, and had never developed on the basis of its own root technologies.

points.h: Anything you do as a follower gets harder the longer you do it
points.body: Fang Xingdong recalls having dinner with Xu Zhijun three years ago, when Xu half muttered to himself: Huawei has done this for so many years, and the finding is that anything you do as a follower always gets harder the longer you do it. There are two kinds of following. In standardized products, Chinese companies can always close the gap and even overtake — but by the time they overtake, there is no profit left in the industry, as with 2G to 5G, PCs and phones. In non-standardized products, such as routers competing with Cisco for so many years, the gap has not closed. In Xu Zhijun's eyes, what Huawei did in the past was also following. That is why Ascend is special among the six products: the other five solve chokehold problems, addressing survival first, while Ascend was not choked in 2019 — it is a fully proactive compute product.

points.h: With process choked off, only system innovation can make it back
points.body: Each generation of industry chips gains roughly 20% or more in performance, mainly from the increase in transistor count driven by advanced process improvements. Huawei lost that premise and can only gain performance through system innovation and breakthroughs — stacked compute, interconnect, higher integration. Fang Xingdong explains with a car metaphor: before, you just had to make the engine stronger and stronger; now the engine has been capped and cannot be enlarged, so you can only make the car run well through architecture, weight reduction and cooling. Nvidia's answer is to keep working on the engine, because TSMC can still manufacture for it. In the interview Liao Heng uses the metaphor of an 18-story pagoda: many companies, because of the great division of labor, are good at only one layer, while Huawei is forced to do manufacturing, ecosystem and chip design all at once.

points.h: Huawei has to pull the domestic supply chain up with it
points.body: Huawei used to do design, relying on the global supply chain, with TSMC manufacturing; for other components it could pick the best international partners, buy American products directly and assemble them, sell at a good price with a brand premium, and earn decent margins. Now cooperation abroad is impossible, TSMC cannot process for it, and domestic processes are still lacking in every respect, so Huawei has no choice but to support and pull up the domestic supply chain — only then does it have a way to survive, only then can its products be manufactured. So the challenge of the past seven years is not just improving its own capabilities but pulling the entire supply chain along — without that, independent self-reliance is impossible. Manufacturing is not Huawei's main business, but it has to help companies like SMIC and Yangtze Memory keep advancing process, yield and quality.

points.h: Ascend's significance is not that Huawei survived, but that the industry has an engine
points.body: In the past, Huawei's product launches and iterations were still based on American root technologies and the industry ecosystem; the high-value components of a phone were basically foreign. Now Huawei's phones, including Ascend, drive an almost 100% domestic supply chain. Fang Xingdong argues the greatest significance of the Tao Law is not that Huawei itself can survive and be self-reliant, but that China's entire semiconductor industry and entire IT industry now has its own engine — something that never existed before. Huawei's rapid growth represents the rapid growth of the whole industry ecosystem. He also points out that the market, reading reports, news or public opinion, has not yet realized that we are at this inflection point — mention Nvidia and people think it is formidable; mention Huawei and they say policy is why everyone uses it.

points.h: It is not a question of difficulty, but of cognition and resolve
points.body: Fang Xingdong argues that doing communications versus doing IT is fundamentally not a question of difficulty but of cognition and resolve — whether you dare to do it. The most typical example is the GaussDB database: among these six products Ascend stood out, and the least conspicuous is probably Gauss, yet the database is a half-century-old industry with a fairly stable market, and being choked on it would be devastating. Huawei at the time wanted to acquire or support a domestic vendor, but after research found none was up to the job; domestic companies could only grow in the cracks left by American giants, with small scale, weak R&D and weak product innovation. So Huawei decided to build it itself, benchmarking Oracle, investing 1 billion, 2 billion, 3 billion yuan a year starting in 2011 and 2012, without knowing whether there would ever be output.

points.h: The future is two centers, not one replacing the other
points.body: Fang Xingdong judges that the shift of global high tech from a single US-centered system to two centers is the general trend; politics will not allow a continued single center — the US will not allow it, and China will not allow it either. He argues a single center is itself abnormal, and only two centers can create competition — only with two systems does every consumer, every company, every country, large or small, have a choice, and not be forced into a binary choice by a chokehold. So the mission of Huawei's six products is to go from being the second choice to being the better choice; the relationship with Nvidia is not simple substitution but each having its strengths, complementing each other, competing and cooperating. He acknowledges the American system is currently stronger, with its advantage mainly in advanced manufacturing, while Huawei, constrained by process, uses the Tao Law to avoid being left behind; once advanced process is also broken through, it can work both tracks at once.

points.h: The tech war won in the short term, at a greater long-term cost
points.body: Fang Xingdong argues the US did indeed suppress Huawei through the tech war, but cannot solve the problem in the long run. He reasons: without the national confrontation of 2017 and 2018, Huawei might be at least a third of Nvidia and a third of Apple, possibly China's largest company by market cap; in 2019 Huawei had already surpassed Apple, and its global shipments briefly exceeded Samsung's for one quarter. Nvidia today stands alone; had it been running neck and neck with Huawei in AI chips from the start, it could not have reached this position. He judges that once the party being attacked builds a self-cycle that does not rely on the outside, and the other side cannot eliminate it even under the harshest conditions, it will be even harder to eliminate later — it will only grow stronger, turning a monopoly into a duopoly.

quotes.text: He said Huawei has done this for so many years, and the finding is that anything you do as a follower always gets harder the longer you do it.
I have been in this industry for 30 years, and I feel that a lot of my past understanding can be reset to zero.
Without the tech war, Huawei is an excellent company, but it might not, would not become a great company; but with the tech war, it will certainly become a great company.

So the few hurdles Huawei faces now are really about technology, but what it drives is the upgrading of China's entire industry, the entire supply chain — yet many things it has to do itself first, because if it doesn't do them, no one else can.
Once the party being attacked — Huawei, say, or China — builds a self-cycle, a self-cycle that does not rely on the outside, frankly it becomes a long-term competitor.
